geniex: geniex geniex qualcomm on-device inference runtime for qualcomm snapdragon that pulls, caches, and runs language and vision-language models on the hexagon npu, adreno gpu, or cpu, dispatching either to llama.cpp with qualcomm's hexagon backend or to the qualcomm ai engine direct runtime, through a cli, an openai-compatible local server, and python, android, and c sdks. represents the geniex software runtime, not the snapdragon silicon it targets and not qualcomm ai hub, the hosted model-compilation and device service from which pre-compiled bundles are fetched. the project was formerly published as nexaai/nexa-sdk; that repository now redirects to qualcomm/geniex, and the reviewed product name and owner are geniex and qualcomm, described in its own documentation as the community version of qualcomm genie. it is not llama.cpp, which it vendors as a submodule and dispatches to, and not qualcomm ai engine direct, the proprietary qualcomm runtime reached through a separate plugin repository. because the product exists to run models on the user's own device and its chat session and local server are how that capability is exercised, it classifies as a runtime rather than an assistant under adr 015. geniex pull downloads a model into a local cache from hugging face, qualcomm ai hub, docker hub, or a local directory or ai hub zip archive, prompting for a gguf precision where several exist and recording an inferred model type. geniex model list enumerates ai hub models with a build for the detected chipset, geniex model set-type rewrites the cached manifest to switch between the language-only and multimodal load path, and geniex config get or set chipset controls chipset detection. gated hugging face repositories are reached through geniex_hftoken, hf_token, or the cached hugging face token file in that priority order. the local server does not auto-download; a model must be pulled first. no removal command is documented. execution is confined to qualcomm snapdragon; the documentation states there is no x86 or non-snapdragon arm build. the validated set is snapdragon x elite and x2 elite on windows arm64, snapdragon 8 elite and 8 elite gen 5 on android, and dragonwing iq-9075 and iq-8275 on linux arm64, with chipset auto-detection on all three and an explicit chipset required for qualcomm ai hub pulls from the android sdk. the llama.cpp runtime reaches the hexagon npu, the adreno gpu through opencl, and the cpu, with a hybrid per-tensor hexagon-plus-cpu scheduler and optional spreading across several htp cores; the qualcomm ai engine direct runtime is npu-only and coerces other compute-unit requests with a warning. python must be an arm64 build. a compute unit is selected per run as npu, gpu, cpu, hybrid, or an explicit htp device list, and sampler and model flags including context length are set on the same command. logging has six levels set by flag or the geniex_log environment variable. speculative decoding is enabled with a draft model and draft-token bounds, and reports an accepted-draft ratio in the profiling block. the bundled server exposes a swagger ui at its root and accepts any non-empty api key without checking it. qualcomm ai engine direct bundles have precision, context length, and kv-cache size baked in and reject attempts to change them at runtime. two runtimes behind one interface give both breadth and depth on the same device: any community gguf from hugging face runs on npu, gpu, or cpu through llama.cpp, while qualcomm ai hub bundles run pre-compiled and pinned to the hexagon npu. model lifecycle is a complete product surface, covering pull from four sources, local cache, precision selection, chipset-aware listing, manifest editing, and gated-repository authentication. the documentation is unusually specific about limits, naming the validated chipset list, the compute-unit alias mapping, the baked-in constraints of pre-compiled bundles, and the exact error returned when audio is sent to an unsupported runtime. hardware coverage is deliberately confined to qualcomm snapdragon, so the runtime cannot serve any other fleet, and the qualcomm ai engine direct path additionally requires a bundle compiled for the specific chipset. serving capability is interactive rather than concurrent: no batching, parallel-request handling, kv-cache management, or distributed serving is documented, and the server performs no authentication. observability is limited to log levels, a benchmarking tool, and per-run throughput output; there is no metrics or health endpoint for an operator. the project is published as a developer preview, and the npu path depends on proprietary qualcomm runtime libraries rather than being open source end to end.
llama-cpp: llama-cpp llama.cpp ggml-org dependency-free c/c++ inference implementation for language and vision-language models, consumed as a library, command-line tool, and bundled openai-compatible server across a wide range of hardware backends. represents the llama.cpp project and the tools it ships. downstream products that embed it, including ollama, lm studio, localai, and jan, are separate boundaries and are not represented by this record. models load from local gguf files or are fetched directly from hugging face through a repository flag. the project provides quantization and conversion tooling rather than a managed local model store. the project documents a backend matrix spanning cpu vector extensions on x86, arm, and risc-v alongside cuda, hip, metal, vulkan, sycl, and further vendor backends. cpu and gpu hybrid inference partially accelerates models larger than available accelerator memory. the bundled server exposes configurable parallel slots, continuous batching, multi-gpu split modes, a prometheus-compatible metrics endpoint, and a slot monitoring endpoint, each settable by flag or environment variable. backend coverage is the broadest in the collection, spanning cpu vector extensions, cuda, hip, metal, vulkan, sycl, and additional vendor backends. the bundled server documents continuous batching, configurable parallel slots, multi-gpu split modes, and prometheus-compatible metrics. distributed execution across machines is available through the project's rpc backend. execution is limited to the project's own gguf format, so weights published in other formats require a conversion step. there is no managed local model store; model retention, naming, and cleanup are the operator's responsibility. capability varies by build configuration, and several documented backends are marked in progress.
lm-studio: lm-studio lm studio element labs desktop application and local server for discovering, downloading, and running language models on a personal machine, with a command-line interface and headless mode for unattended hosts. represents the local model runner and its server. its chat window is how local execution is exercised rather than a broad conversational workspace with durable projects and connected information, so the product is curated as a runtime rather than an assistant. models are discovered and downloaded from hugging face inside the application and managed through its interface or the lms command-line tool, which also controls the daemon and server. documented requirements cover apple silicon on macos 14 or newer, x64 systems with avx2 and arm snapdragon x elite on windows, and x64 or arm64 on ubuntu 20.04 or newer. intel-based macs are not supported and at least 4 gb of dedicated video memory is recommended on windows. inference runtimes are selected automatically per model and can be managed and updated from a dedicated runtimes surface. the server can be started and stopped from the application or the command-line tool. ships llama.cpp engine variants for cpu, cuda, vulkan, rocm, and metal alongside an apple mlx engine, selecting an engine and offload parameters automatically. model discovery, download, and management are integrated into one interface with a command-line equivalent. provides a headless mode for servers and continuous-integration hosts in addition to the desktop application. the application core is proprietary; only the command-line tool and client sdks are published under an open license. execution is limited to gguf and mlx weights, and mlx is available only on apple silicon. operational visibility is confined to in-application server logs, with no documented metrics endpoint.
localai: localai localai ettore di giacinto and contributors self-hosted server presenting compatible text, embedding, image, and audio apis over interchangeable local inference backends, with a model gallery and a web interface. represents the self-hosted gateway and the backends it manages, not the individual inference engines it can load and not any hosted service. models are installed from a built-in gallery through the web interface or the command-line tool, and backends are downloaded automatically to match detected hardware. dedicated container images cover cpu-only operation alongside nvidia, amd, intel, and vulkan acceleration. the project documents automatic detection of available gpu capability and states that a gpu is not required. a built-in web interface manages installations and configuration. a distributed mode registers gpu worker nodes with a front-end coordinator for scaling beyond one host. presents openai-compatible, anthropic messages, and open responses apis over one self-hosted endpoint, spanning text, embeddings, images, and audio. a model gallery plus automatic backend selection removes most manual setup for mixed hardware. documents container, orchestrated, and distributed multi-node deployment paths. capability depends on which backend serves a given model, so behaviour is not uniform across the catalogue. as a gateway it inherits the limits of the engines it loads rather than optimising execution itself. published operational visibility is centred on the web interface rather than a documented metrics surface.
mlc-llm: mlc-llm mlc llm mlc ai community machine-learning compiler and deployment engine that converts and compiles language models into platform-native binaries, then executes them on mlcengine through python, a command line, a rest server, and swift and kotlin sdks across desktop gpus and phones. represents the mlc llm package, its conversion and compilation tooling, and the mlcengine runtime, distributed as the python package, cli, rest server, and ios/android sdks built from this repository. it is not apache tvm, the general-purpose tensor compiler and tensorir stack it is built on and installs as a separate dependency; tvm supplies the code generation, while this record covers the model definitions, quantization schemes, engine, and serving surfaces layered above it. it is also not webllm: mlc-ai/web-llm is a separately maintained, versioned, and licensed package with its own record that runs mlcengine inside a browser through webgpu; both consume the same compiled mlc model format, but only mlc-ai/mlc-llm's own release is scored here. the ios and android chat applications built from this repository are demonstrations of the sdks, not an assistant workspace, so the origins, methods, headers, and credentials are configurable. there is no authentication, metrics endpoint, or health endpoint. one compiler and one engine target an unusually wide set of execution surfaces — desktop gpus on three operating systems plus ios and android phones — with the same openai-compatible interface on each. compilation is a first-class, documented workflow: weight conversion, quantization configuration, model-library compilation, packaging for mobile builds, and defining a new model architecture each have their own reference page. the server exposes tensor-parallel sharding, prefix caching, configurable batch sizing through engine modes, and three families of speculative decoding without requiring a separate orchestrator. nothing runs without pointed at and served directly. operational visibility is minimal, with per-request tracing and a cli statistics command but no metrics endpoint, health endpoint, authentication, container image, or orchestration guidance. the supported model architecture list is narrower than mainstream server engines, and the published documentation is still versioned 0.1.0 with pages of differing freshness, so capability must be confirmed per model and per release.
mlx-lm: mlx-lm mlx lm apple machine learning research python package for generating text with and fine-tuning language models on apple silicon through the mlx array framework, usable as a library, command-line tool, and small local server. represents the language-model package rather than the underlying mlx array framework, and covers apple silicon execution only. models are fetched from the hugging face hub by identifier, and the package can quantize models and upload the result back to the hub. prompt caches persist to disk for reuse across generations. execution targets apple silicon through mlx. no other accelerator or operating system is supported. generation and sampling parameters are set per command or per call. distributed execution is available through the mlx distributed interface. first-party apple silicon execution path with quantization, upload, and low-rank or full fine-tuning in one package. hugging face hub integration reaches a large published catalogue of mlx-compatible models with a single command. usable as a python module, a set of command-line tools, and a local server without additional components. apple silicon is the only supported target, so the package cannot serve mixed or non-apple fleets. the bundled server is explicitly documented as not recommended for production because it implements only basic security checks. serving capability is minimal, with no documented continuous batching, metrics, or administrative surface.
ollama: ollama ollama ollama local model runner that packages model download, storage, and serving behind one cli, desktop application, and rest api on the user's own hardware. represents the self-operated ollama runtime. ollama cloud, the hosted tier operated by the same organization, is a separate managed inference service record. the model library ollama distributes is not part of this record. models are pulled, pushed, created from a modelfile, copied, listed, and deleted through the cli and rest api. safetensors weights and adapters can be imported into the local store. documented nvidia support requires compute capability 5.0 or newer with driver 550 or newer; amd support runs through rocm; apple silicon runs through metal. models that do not fit one accelerator are spread across available gpus, and available memory governs how many models load concurrently. server environment variables govern loaded-model count, parallel requests per model, and queue depth. cuda_visible_devices restricts gpu selection. running models and versions are inspectable through the api. model lifecycle management is unusually complete for a local runner, covering pull, push, create, copy, import, and delete through both cli and api. documents openai-compatible and anthropic-compatible endpoints alongside its native api, plus embeddings, tool calling, structured outputs, and vision. installers, container images, and hardware support are documented per platform with explicit driver and compute-capability floors. concurrency is limited to parallel request slots and multiple loaded models; the documentation describes no continuous batching or distributed serving. documented accelerator coverage spans nvidia, amd, and apple silicon; vulkan and intel paths are not part of the published hardware support matrix. operational visibility is limited to running-model and version endpoints with no documented metrics endpoint.

only in-process profiling and logging, so operational visibility depends entirely on the host application. the continuous-batching engine api is documented as a transitional host-facing surface that is not thread-safe, and the published support matrix still lists speculative decoding as roadmap while the repository documents it as implemented, so capability varies by version and build.
openvino-model-server: openvino-model-server openvino model server intel c++ inference server that serves generative and classic deep-learning models compiled by openvino onto intel cpu, gpu, and npu plugins, model conversion, and optimization tooling and is a separate boundary, as are the openvino genai library and the models published in intel's hugging face collections. the server is headless and operated as a container, a binary package, a windows service, or an in-process c api host; it ships no graphical or conversational interface, which keeps it on the runtime side of the adr 015 runtime-versus-assistant test. models live in a versioned model repository on local storage, s3, google cloud storage, azure blob, or the hugging face hub. a pull mode downloads models in openvino ir or gguf form without starting the service, and a conversion path exports and quantizes pytorch sources through optimum-cli. version policies choose which numbered versions are served, configuration changes and new or removed models are applied at runtime without restarting, and a model cache speeds repeated loads. execution targets intel hardware: x86 cpus including xeon, intel integrated and discrete gpus through the openvino gpu plugin built on onednn and opencl, and npu devices, on linux and windows as containers or binary packages. gpu and npu use requires host drivers and, for containers, the accelerator-enabled image and device passthrough. npu execution uses the stateful pipeline and static shapes only, so dynamic models must be reset with a fixed batch size or shape, while cpu and gpu use the continuous-batching pipeline. the server takes device selection per model through target_device, including hetero and auto virtual devices with latency, throughput, and cumulative-throughput hints. llm graphs configure kv-cache size, maximum active sequences, dynamic split fuse, prefix caching, and cache eviction. generative endpoints can require a bearer api key from a file or environment variable, and request limits cover execution streams, grpc threads, rest workers, message size, and memory quota. one server presents openai-compatible chat, completions, responses, embeddings, image generation, and audio endpoints, a cohere-compatible rerank api, and kserve and tensorflow serving apis over both rest and grpc. generative serving uses continuous batching and paged attention with prefix caching, cache eviction, dynamic split fuse, and draft-model speculative decoding, and classic models run through a dag scheduler and mediapipe graphs. operations are mature: prometheus-compatible metrics with a documented metric list, versioned model repositories on cloud storage, runtime configuration reload, docker, bare-metal, windows service, kubernetes and openshift deployment, and a c api for in-process embedding. hardware coverage is intel-only; there is no documented cuda, rocm, or metal execution path, so the server does not serve mixed-vendor accelerator fleets. generative models are normally served from openvino ir exported with optimum-cli, gguf support is limited to text generation on a published model list, and npu serving requires static shapes. the documentation states that grpc and rest endpoints provide no access restrictions or traffic encryption by default, with an api key available only for the generative /v3 endpoints, so production exposure depends on a reverse proxy; scaling beyond one host is by replicas rather than multi-host model parallelism.
sglang: sglang sglang sglang project serving engine for language and multimodal models built around radix-tree prefix caching, continuous batching, and multi-accelerator parallelism on operator-controlled hardware. represents the self-hosted serving engine and its runtime, not the models it serves and not any managed platform that deploys it for a customer. models load from hugging face repositories or local paths at launch, with adapter support. the engine does not provide a managed local model store. documented execution covers nvidia and amd accelerators, intel xeon processors, google tpu, and ascend npu targets, with published configuration recipes for specific data-centre accelerator families. parallelism strategy, prefix caching, and speculative decoding are configured at launch, and container images support orchestrated deployment. radix-tree prefix caching, continuous batching, and tensor, pipeline, and data parallelism are documented as core scheduling capabilities. accelerator coverage extends beyond nvidia and amd to intel xeon, google tpu, and ascend npu targets. native multimodal handling covers text, image, video, and audio alongside structured output and tool calling. targets accelerator-backed server deployment with no desktop packaging or graphical interface. documentation is oriented toward data-centre accelerators, so consumer-hardware guidance is thinner than in desktop-first runtimes. model selection is fixed at launch, and the engine provides no local model lifecycle management.
tensorflow-serving: tensorflow-serving tensorflow serving google production model server that loads versioned savedmodel servables from a watched model directory and answers predict, classify, regress, and metadata calls over a grpc-first interface with a mirrored rest surface. represents the tensorflow_model_server binary and the serving libraries in the tensorflow/serving repository, not the tensorflow framework in tensorflow/tensorflow. the framework builds and trains models and supplies the session runtime this server links against; the server's own documentation states that it deals with the inference aspect of machine learning, taking models after training and managing their lifetimes, which is the separate product this record reviews. tensorflow lite and litert are a different execution stack for mobile and embedded targets and are out of scope here; the server carries only an experimental --prefer_tflite_model flag that picks up a model.tflite file inside a savedmodel directory, which the flag text marks as removable at any time. managed google cloud offerings that host this server for customers, including vertex ai prebuilt tensorflow prediction containers, hold the serving contract themselves and are inference-service boundaries rather than part of this record. the server is headless, operated as a container, an apt-installed binary, or a kubernetes deployment, and ships no graphical or conversational interface, which keeps it on the runtime side of the adr 015 runtime-versus-assistant test. models are staged by the operator as numbered version directories under a model_base_path; there is no fetch, pull, registry, or removal command. the server polls the filesystem on --file_system_poll_wait_seconds and loads new versions automatically. a modelserverconfig file names multiple models and sets a model_version_policy of latest, specific versions, or all, and version_labels attach names such as stable and canary that clients address through the request modelspec or a /v1/models/<name>/labels/<label> rest path. the config is reloaded either by polling --model_config_file_poll_wait_seconds or through a handlereloadconfigrequest rpc, and the server realizes only the new config, so a model absent from it is unloaded. version policies are availability preserving or resource preserving, load and unload run on sized thread pools with retry settings, and savedmodel warmup replays predictionlogs from assets.extra at load time. there is no adapter or lora mechanism; custom model types enter through c++ source, sourceadapter, and loader extension points. documented execution is cpu and nvidia gpu on linux. the apt channel publishes tensorflow-model-server, built with platform-specific sse4 and avx instructions, and tensorflow-model-server-universal for machines without them; the documentation states that only linux binaries are supported when building from source. gpu serving uses the tensorflow/serving:latest-gpu image, current nvidia drivers, and nvidia-docker or docker --gpus. there is no documented rocm, metal, vulkan, npu, or directml path, and no documented multi-gpu or multi-host model-parallel serving; scale beyond one process is by replicas. the binary carries a --skip_initialize_tpu flag and experimental --xla_cpu_compilation_enabled, --xla_gpu_compilation_enabled, and --mixed_precision=bfloat16 flags whose behaviour is described in the source rather than in the published guides. batching is off by default and enabled with --enable_batching plus a batchingparameters file setting max_batch_size, batch_timeout_micros, num_batch_threads, max_enqueued_batches, and optional allowed_batch_sizes; scheduling is global across all models and versions on the server unless --enable_per_model_batching_parameters is set. concurrency and resource limits cover rest_api_num_threads, rest_api_timeout_in_ms, grpc_max_threads, tensorflow_session_parallelism with intra- and inter-op settings, a thread_pool_factory_config_file, and per_process_gpu_memory_fraction. transport security is configured through an sslconfig file for the grpc channel and optional google alts credentials; the rest surface has no documented tls or authentication and offers only cors headers, so public exposure depends on a proxy. observability is a monitoringconfig that enables a prometheus endpoint at a configured path collecting both serving and core tensorflow metrics, a model status api on rest and grpc, an optional standard grpc health-check service, sampled request logging, and a profiler service consumed through tensorboard. version handling is the most developed in the collection: numbered version directories, latest, specific, and all version policies, string version labels for canary and rollback addressable from both apis, availability- or resource-preserving load ordering, and config reload by polling or rpc without restarting the server. the request batching scheduler is separately documented and tunable, schedules globally across every loaded model and version, and can be limited to a fixed set of allowed batch sizes. the grpc predictionservice and modelservice protos and their mirrored rest endpoints are stable, versioned, and specific enough that other servers reimplement them as a compatibility surface. operational surfaces are complete for a classic server: prometheus metrics, model status and metadata endpoints, a grpc health check, sampled request logging, a tensorboard profiler, container and apt install paths with a documented upgrade command, and a kubernetes deployment guide. accelerator coverage is cpu and nvidia gpu on linux only, with no support matrix published and no rocm, metal, vulkan, or npu path. the server executes tensorflow savedmodel graphs and nothing else; there is no conversion tooling of its own, no quantization scheme it applies, and the only other loadable artifact is a model.tflite file behind a flag the source marks as experimental and removable. the api is deliberately tensor-shaped: predict, classify, regress, and multi-inference with no streaming, no embeddings endpoint, no tool calling, and no structured output, and no openai- or anthropic-compatible surface, so llm clients cannot address it without an adapter. there is no kv-cache management and no distributed or multi-host serving; a large model must fit the process, and scale is by replicas. rest has no documented authentication or transport security, and several published pages are dated: the documentation site renders under tensorflow v2.16.1 while releases have reached 2.20.0, gpu instructions still reference nvidia-docker, and the flag reference defers to main.cc for anything beyond a short list.
tensorrt-llm: tensorrt-llm tensorrt llm nvidia nvidia inference and serving engine for language, multimodal, and visual generation models, combining custom gpu kernels, a pytorch-native runtime, and an optional ahead-of-time compiled tensorrt engine path behind one python llm api and an openai-compatible server. represents the tensorrt llm library and its trtllm-serve, trtllm-bench, and trtllm-eval tools, operated on gpus the user controls. it is not tensorrt, the general-purpose nvidia deep-learning inference library and engine-builder it can compile through, and it is not nvidia's managed offerings, which hold their own serving contract and belong to the inference-service collection. nvidia dynamo and triton inference server orchestrate this engine and are separate boundaries, as is nvidia model optimizer, the offline quantization toolkit whose checkpoints this runtime loads. models are named by hugging face repository identifier or local checkpoint directory at engine construction, with a pluggable checkpoint-loading architecture that separates config loader, weight loader, and weight mapper so a new checkpoint format can be added without changing the engine. pre-quantized checkpoints produced by nvidia model optimizer load directly; offline quantization is a separate step in that project. multiple lora adapters are supported per request. there is no runtime model store, pinning, or removal command, and the legacy tensorrt backend additionally requires an engine build step whose artifact is specific to the gpu architecture and parallelism configuration it was built for. the published support matrix limits the reviewed runtime to linux on x86_64 or aarch64 with nvidia gpus from the ampere, ada lovelace, hopper, grace hopper, and blackwell architectures including gb200 nvl72; architectures outside that list are community-supported only. available precisions vary by architecture, with fp8 documented from ada lovelace onward and int4 awq or gptq with fp8 activations requiring compute capability 8.9 or higher. windows and macos are not supported, and a jetson path exists only on a separate release branch. parallelism is configured at launch through tensor, pipeline, expert, context, and data-parallel sizes, alongside kv-cache dtype and block reuse, chunked prefill, cuda graph batch sizes, scheduler policy, and speculative decoding mode. trtllm-serve exposes /health, /metrics, and /version, with the metrics endpoint reporting runtime iteration statistics including gpu memory use and in-flight batching detail. anonymous telemetry is collected by default and can be disabled by environment variable, a marker file, a python config field, or a cli flag. a stated deprecation policy gives a three-month migration window with runtime warnings. serving capability is unusually complete, covering in-flight batching, paged kv cache with block reuse, chunked prefill, an overlap scheduler, prefill-decode disaggregation, and tensor, pipeline, expert, context, and data parallelism across single-node and multi-node deployments. quantization coverage is broad and documented per model, spanning nvfp4, mxfp4, several fp8 recipes, fp8 and nvfp4 kv cache, and w4a8 or w4a16 awq and gptq, with a published model-by-model support table. the server implements openai chat, completions, and responses endpoints plus a dedicated embeddings subcommand with dynamic batching, alongside guided decoding, multi-lora serving, and multimodal input. execution is confined to nvidia gpus on linux; there is no cpu, amd, apple, or windows execution path in the reviewed support matrix, so the runtime cannot serve a mixed fleet. the project carries two backends whose model coverage differs, and the current pytorch backend is primary while the tensorrt engine-building path is documented separately, so a capability confirmed for one backend is not evidence for the other. several headline features are labelled beta or prototype in the documentation, including disaggregated serving and autodeploy, and the published support matrix page is stamped almost a year older than the installation guide, so version-specific verification is required. the repository ships a visual-generation model directory under a restricted community license with revenue-based commercial terms, so redistribution and commercial use of the whole tree are not uniformly apache-2.0.
text-embeddings-inference: text-embeddings-inference text embeddings inference hugging face a rust-based inference server purpose-built for serving text embedding, sparse embedding, sequence-classification, and reranking models on operator-controlled hardware. represents the self-hosted text embeddings inference server. hugging face inference endpoints, which can deploy this server on hugging face's managed infrastructure, is a separate service boundary. text generation inference is hugging face's sibling runtime for causal language-model generation; its repository is archived and excluded from this collection, and this record does not stand in for it, since embedding, classification, and reranking are a distinct workload from generation. models are pulled from hugging face hub repositories by model id and revision, or loaded from a local directory produced by transformers' or sentence transformers' save_pretrained. an hf_token grants access to private or gated repositories, and a documented air-gapped path mounts pre-downloaded weights as a volume; there is no runtime-managed model store beyond the shared hugging face hub cache. documented images target x86_64 and aarch64 cpus, with dedicated onnx and intel mkl backends, nvidia gpus from turing through blackwell (cuda compute capability 7.5 or higher; volta and older are unsupported), apple silicon through metal, and amd instinct gpus through rocm, which the project marks experimental. startup flags bound concurrency and batching (--max-concurrent-requests, --max-batch-tokens, --max-batch-requests, --max-client-batch-size), gate access with --api-key, and configure payload limits and cors. the server exposes prometheus metrics on a dedicated port, opentelemetry distributed tracing, and /health and /info endpoints for operators. serves dense embeddings, splade sparse embeddings, sequence classification, and cross-encoder reranking from one runtime, through dedicated /embed, /embed_sparse, /rerank, /predict, and /similarity endpoints alongside an openai-compatible /v1/embeddings route. ships prebuilt docker images tuned to specific gpu architectures (turing, ampere, ada lovelace, hopper, blackwell) plus cpu, arm64, and experimental rocm images, so operators can match a container to their exact hardware. production-oriented observability is built in: prometheus metrics, opentelemetry tracing, and a grpc api as a high-throughput alternative to http. model format support is narrower than generative-model runtimes: only safetensors and onnx weight loading are documented, with no quantization-format ecosystem comparable to gguf, awq, or gptq. there is no documented multi-gpu or distributed-serving mode; scaling beyond one accelerator means running and load-balancing multiple instances rather than a runtime-native parallelism strategy. rocm support is explicitly experimental, and gpus below cuda compute capability 7.5 are unsupported.
vllm: vllm vllm vllm project high-throughput inference and serving engine built around paged attention, continuous batching, and multi-dimensional parallelism for operator-controlled accelerators. represents the self-hosted serving engine. managed services that deploy vllm on a customer's behalf are separate inference-service boundaries, and the models it serves are not part of this record. models load from hugging face repositories or local paths at server start, with adapter and quantization support. weights are pinned by the launch configuration rather than managed through a runtime model store. documented execution covers nvidia gpus, amd gpus, and x86, arm, and powerpc cpus, with further accelerators available through a plugin architecture that includes tpu, gaudi, spyre, and ascend targets. parallelism strategy, batching, prefix caching, and speculative decoding are configured at launch. the project documents an observability surface for a running server alongside distributed deployment guidance. serving capability is the most complete in the collection, covering continuous batching, chunked prefill, prefix caching, and tensor, pipeline, data, expert, and context parallelism. quantization and weight-format coverage spans fp8, mxfp8, nvfp4, int8, int4, gptq, awq, gguf, and compressed-tensors. serves an openai-compatible api alongside an anthropic messages api and grpc, with structured outputs and tool calling. the engine targets accelerator-backed server deployment; it is not packaged as a desktop application and has no graphical interface. accelerators beyond nvidia and amd depend on plugins whose maturity varies by target. model selection is fixed by launch configuration, so changing weights means restarting or running another instance.
web-llm: web-llm webllm mlc ai community in-browser llm inference engine built on mlcengine that runs entirely client-side through webgpu, exposing an openai-compatible javascript and typescript api with streaming, json-mode structured generation, and web worker, service worker, and browser-extension integration. represents the mlc-ai/web-llm package: its typescript api, prebuilt-model registry, and the browser-side mlcengine that runs entirely inside a web page through webgpu and webassembly, with no local server process. it is published, versioned, and licensed separately from mlc-ai/mlc-llm, the sibling record covering the python compiler, cli, and rest server; both consume the same compiled mlc model format, but a genuinely new model architecture still depends on mlc-llm's python compilation pipeline to produce the wasm model library this package loads. webllm chat (chat.webllm.ai) and the community web-llm-chat project are demonstration and third-party chat applications built on this engine, not part of the reviewed package, so it stays on the runtime side of the adr 015 test. prebuilt models are referenced by id against webllm.prebuiltappconfig.model_list (for example llama-3-8b-instruct-q4f32_1-mlc), which points at mlc-quantized weights hosted on the hugging face hub and a matching webgpu-targeted wasm model library; the browser fetches and reuses both, though official docs do not specify the underlying cache api or eviction behavior. a new quantized variant of an already-supported architecture can be registered as a custom modelrecord pointing at hub-hosted weights without local compilation; a genuinely new architecture still requires running mlc_llm compile with the separate python package to produce a new wasm model library before it can be registered the same way. there is no documented command to list, pin, or remove cached model artifacts from within the library itself. the only documented requirement is a webgpu-capable browser; the project points users at a recent chrome release and an external webgpu support-check tool. no cpu-only fallback, minimum vram, or non-chrome compatibility matrix is stated in official sources, so behavior on other webgpu-shipping browsers is unconfirmed. the javascript api exposes chat-completion parameters including temperature, json-mode and grammar-constrained structured generation, and streaming, plus explicit engine construction options for web worker and service worker offload and progress callbacks during model loading. there is no documented authentication, metrics endpoint, health endpoint, or request-level tracing; the runtime executes inside the host page's own security context and origin. runs a full openai-compatible chat-completion api, including streaming and json-mode structured generation, entirely client-side with no inference server to operate or secure. first-class web worker, service worker, and chrome-extension integration patterns let a host application offload inference off the main thread without a separate runtime process. reuses mlc llm's compiled model libraries and hugging face-hosted quantized weights, so architectures already supported by the desktop engine reach the browser without a parallel compilation effort. execution is documented against a single accelerator path, webgpu in chrome, with no stated cpu fallback or cross-browser compatibility matrix from official sources. serving is inherently single-stream, one browser tab per user, with no batching, request queuing, or multi-user concurrency of any kind. a genuinely new model architecture still depends on mlc-llm's separate python compiler to produce a wasm model library, so the package cannot originate full compilation support on its own. no authentication, metrics endpoint, health endpoint, or request tracing is documented; observability is whatever the host web application builds around the library.
xinference: xinference xinference xorbits self-hosted supervisor-and-worker server that launches language, embedding, reranking, image, audio, and multimodal models on interchangeable inference backends and presents them through one openai-compatible api, a web interface, a command line, and a python client. represents the self-hosted community edition and the backends it launches, not the engines themselves: vllm, sglang, llama.cpp through xllamacpp, mlx, and transformers each keep their own boundary, and vllm has its own record. it is distinct from localai, the other reviewed compatibility gateway, which ships its own go server with bundled c++ backends and a gallery aimed at a single mixed-hardware host, whereas xinference is a python cluster of a supervisor and workers that places model replicas across machines. xinference enterprise and the maintainer's hosted plans hold the serving contract for their customers and are outside this record. the bundled web interface is a management and test console for locally launched models, not a conversational workspace, so the record stays on the runtime side of the adr 015 runtime-versus-assistant test. the separately licensed enterprise edition and the maintainer's hosted plans are outside this record. a built-in catalogue launches models by name with one command, downloading from hugging face or modelscope and caching files locally for later starts. custom models are registered from a local path or a json specification, cached files are listed and removed through the command line and web interface, running models are terminated to free resources, and lora modules are attached at launch from operator-supplied paths. per-model virtual environments isolate backend dependencies, and the backend is selected automatically from model format, quantization, and hardware unless the operator names one. installation is documented on linux, windows, and macos with backend extras installed per model type. cuda devices are required for the vllm and sglang backends, the mlx backend targets apple silicon, llama.cpp covers cpu and gpu hosts with automatic gpu-layer estimation, and ascend npu execution is documented through torch-npu with the transformers backend only, which the project states is slow on some chips and steers to its enterprise mindie engine. multi-gpu and multi-node execution is available for the engines that support it. models launch with a chosen engine, replica count, gpu count, and optional per-replica placement onto named workers. a database-backed authentication system with users, permissions, api keys, and optional oidc single sign-on is enabled by default and can be disabled by environment variable. supervisor and worker prometheus metrics exporters, cluster start and stop commands, and a web interface complete the operator surface. one openai-compatible endpoint covers chat, completions, embeddings, reranking, image, audio, and multimodal models launched from a large built-in catalogue with a single command. cluster operation is first class: a supervisor with registered workers, replica placement, distributed inference across machines on vllm, sglang, and mlx, and shared kv cache between vllm replicas. operational controls are unusually complete for a gateway, with database-backed authentication and api keys enabled by default, oidc single sign-on, supervisor and worker metrics exporters, and per-model virtual environments. execution quality, batching, and quantization coverage come from the selected backend, so behaviour is not uniform across the catalogue and each backend carries its own installation constraints. ascend npu support in the open-source edition runs only on the transformers backend, and the project directs users needing the mindie engine to a separately licensed enterprise edition. the python dependency surface is heavy and version-sensitive, with vllm and sglang documented as conflicting inside one environment and several backends requiring separate installation commands.
